title: How the Books Were Chosen
summary: How the Old and New Testaments came to contain the books they do, why some Bibles include the Apocrypha, what the early church looked for in a book, and how scholars and traditions explain the process.

sections.body:
The list of books a community receives as Scripture is called its canon. The word comes from the Greek kanōn, a straight rod or measuring stick, and so a rule or standard. Early Christian writers spoke of the ‘rule of faith’, the summary of apostolic teaching by which doctrine was measured, and in the fourth century the word began to be used for the list of books themselves. Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter of 367, spoke of the books that are ‘canonized’, and from then on canon in this sense became standard.

The word can mean two things, and much confusion comes from mixing them. It can mean a closed list: these books and no others. It can also mean a body of writings that functions with authority in a community, whether or not anyone has drawn up a list. In the second sense, the Law of Moses was canonical for Israel long before anyone counted the books of the Hebrew Bible, and the Gospels and Paul's letters were functioning as Scripture in the churches of the second century long before any council ruled on them. Scholars who say the canon was formed ‘late’ usually mean the closed list; scholars who say it was formed ‘early’ usually mean functioning authority. Both can be right.

There is also a theological question underneath the historical one. Did the church create the canon, conferring authority on books by choosing them, or did it recognize a canon, acknowledging an authority the books already had? Protestant writers such as Bruce Metzger (The Canon of the New Testament, 1987) and F. F. Bruce (The Canon of Scripture, 1988) insisted on the second: the church did not make these books Scripture but received them as such. Michael Kruger (Canon Revisited, 2012) argues that the canon is in a sense self-authenticating, its authority shown in its apostolic origin, its consistency with the rest of Scripture, and its reception by the church. Catholic theology agrees that the books are inspired by God, not made so by the church, and adds that the church, guided by the Spirit, has the authority to define which books they are. Critical historians such as Lee Martin McDonald (The Formation of the Biblical Canon, 2017) emphasize how fluid the boundaries were for centuries and how much the process owed to use in worship and to the needs of particular communities. These are different questions, and the history below is compatible with more than one answer.

sections.h: The Hebrew Bible: Law, Prophets, and Writings
sections.body:
The Old Testament took shape in layers, and the order of its three parts roughly reflects the order in which they came to be treated as a closed collection. The Torah, the five books of Moses, stood first and alone. When Ezra read the Book of the Law to the returned exiles in Jerusalem in the fifth century BC, the Levites explained it, “so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8). The Samaritans, who separated from the Jerusalem community in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, kept only the Torah as Scripture, which suggests its authority was settled before the split.

The Prophets followed. Around 132 BC the grandson of Jesus ben Sira, translating his grandfather's book of wisdom into Greek, wrote a prologue that refers three times to the law, the prophets, and the other books of the ancestors. That is the earliest clear witness to a threefold collection, with the third part not yet given a fixed name. In the New Testament, Jesus speaks of the Law and the Prophets as a unit (Matthew 5:17) and once of “the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). Around AD 95 the Jewish historian Josephus, in Against Apion 1.37-43, describes the Jewish books as a fixed number, twenty-two, from Moses to the reign of Artaxerxes, and says that nothing has been added or taken away since the succession of prophets ended; his twenty-two probably equal the later twenty-four, with Ruth joined to Judges and Lamentations to Jeremiah. The apocalypse known as 4 Ezra, from about the same time, speaks of twenty-four public books. The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) gives the order of the Prophets and Writings, and the Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records rabbis still debating in the second century whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes ‘defile the hands’, their technical way of asking whether a book is holy Scripture; the ruling was that both do.

For much of the twentieth century textbooks taught that a ‘Council of Jamnia’ (Yavneh) around AD 90 closed the Hebrew canon. The idea goes back to the historian Heinrich Graetz in 1871. Jack P. Lewis's article of 1964, ‘What Do We Mean by Jabneh?’, and the later work of Sid Z. Leiman showed that there was no council in the sense of a body issuing a list, only rabbinic discussion of a few books already in use. Scholars now divide over when the list was effectively closed. Roger Beckwith (The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church, 1985) argued that the twenty-four books were settled before the time of Jesus, pointing among other things to Jesus' words about the blood of the righteous “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35), which may run from the first murder in Genesis to the last in Chronicles, the final book in the Hebrew order. Others, including Timothy Lim (The Formation of the Jewish Canon, 2013) and James Sanders, argue that different Jewish communities used different collections until after AD 70, with the Pharisaic list becoming the rabbinic canon over the following centuries. The Dead Sea Scrolls add evidence on both sides: they contain every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, and the community also treasured books such as Jubilees and 1 Enoch.

The books in dispute between Protestants and Catholics were written by Jews between about 300 BC and AD 100, most of them in Hebrew or Aramaic, though several survive only in Greek. They include history (1 Maccabees, the main source for the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in the 160s BC), edifying stories (Tobit, Judith), and wisdom (Sirach, written around 180 BC, and the Wisdom of Solomon). They were copied in the great Greek Bibles of the church: the fourth- and fifth-century codices Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and Alexandrinus all contain some of them, though not the same selection.

The early church read them, quoted them, and in the Latin West largely received them. Augustine regarded them as Scripture, and the North African councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) listed them with the other books of the Old Testament. Jerome, who learned Hebrew and translated the Old Testament from it around 390 to 405, argued that the church should hold as canonical only what the Jews held, and that the other books could be read for edification but not to establish doctrine. Earlier, Melito of Sardis (whose list Eusebius preserves in Ecclesiastical History 4.26) and Athanasius (in 367) gave Old Testament lists close to the Hebrew canon, though Athanasius also included Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah and placed Esther among the books to be read. The question stayed open through the Middle Ages, with some Catholic scholars, including Cardinal Cajetan in the early sixteenth century, following Jerome.

The Reformation made the question urgent, partly because 2 Maccabees 12 was cited in support of prayer for the dead and purgatory. Luther's Bible of 1534 gathered the books in a separate section between the testaments with a heading describing them as not equal to Holy Scripture but useful and good to read. The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (Article 6, 1563 and 1571) say much the same, quoting Jerome. The Westminster Confession (1646) went further, declaring them not inspired and of no more authority than other human writings. The Council of Trent, on 8 April 1546, defined the full list, including the deuterocanonical books, as sacred and canonical. The Orthodox, at the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672, also affirmed them, with a slightly larger Septuagint list.

The New Testament never quotes any of these books with the formulas it uses for Scripture, such as ‘it is written’, though it shows knowledge of Jewish traditions found in them; Hebrews 11:35, for instance, seems to recall the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7. Jude 14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a book outside every canon except the Ethiopian. Protestants take the absence of formal quotation, together with the Hebrew canon Jesus' contemporaries used, as evidence for the shorter list. Catholics and Orthodox point to the church's long use of the Greek Old Testament, which the apostles quoted, and to the councils of the fourth century. Both sides agree that the dispute concerns the Old Testament's edges, not its center.

sections.h: The New Testament: from letters to Scripture
sections.body:
The earliest Christians already had a Bible, the Scriptures of Israel. What they added was, first, the words of Jesus, handed down orally and quoted with supreme authority (Paul cites a command of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 7:10 and the words of the Last Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:23-25). Then came the apostles' writings. Paul expected his letters to be read aloud in the assembly and passed between churches: “After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans” (Colossians 4:16). Within the New Testament itself, 2 Peter 3:16 places Paul's letters alongside “the rest of the Scriptures”, and 1 Timothy 5:18 quotes a saying found in Luke 10:7 next to a verse of Deuteronomy under the heading ‘the Scripture says’.

By the early second century, collections were forming. Paul's letters circulated as a set: the papyrus codex known as P46, copied around AD 200, contains Romans, Hebrews, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians, and 1 Thessalonians in a single book. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around 150, says that on Sundays Christians read the memoirs of the apostles, which he says are called Gospels, or the writings of the prophets. Around 180, Irenaeus of Lyon argued in Against Heresies (3.11.8) that there are four Gospels and could be no more or fewer, as there are four winds and four corners of the world; the argument is odd to modern ears, but it shows the fourfold Gospel was settled in his churches. Tatian, his contemporary, wove the four into a single narrative, the Diatessaron, which also shows that these four and no others were the material to work with.

The pressure of rival teachers sharpened the question. Around 140 Marcion, a wealthy shipowner from Pontus, came to Rome teaching that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser being than the Father of Jesus. He issued his own collection: an edited Gospel of Luke and ten letters of Paul, cut to remove what he thought Jewish additions. Hans von Campenhausen (The Formation of the Christian Bible, German 1968, English 1972) argued that Marcion's canon forced the great church to define its own; others, including Kruger, reply that Marcion was editing a collection already in use, and that the church's response defended books it already had. In the later second century came the Gnostic teachers, who produced gospels of their own and claimed secret traditions from the apostles; the church answered by pointing to public writings and public succession of teachers in the churches the apostles founded.

The earliest surviving list is the Muratorian Fragment, a damaged Latin copy of an older list, discovered in Milan and published by Ludovico Antonio Muratori in 1740. It accepts the four Gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, and Revelation, adds the Wisdom of Solomon, mentions an Apocalypse of Peter that some would not read in church, and says the Shepherd of Hermas may be read privately but not publicly because it was written recently. Most scholars date it to the late second century in or near Rome; Albert Sundberg (1973) and Geoffrey Hahneman (The Muratorian Fragment and the Development of the Canon, 1992) argued for the fourth century in the East. The majority date has held, but the debate is a live one.

sections.h: The fourth century and the settled list
sections.body:
By around 200 the core of the New Testament was agreed across the churches: the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul, 1 Peter, and 1 John. Questions remained about a handful of shorter or later-circulating books. Origen of Alexandria in the third century noted which books were disputed. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing his Ecclesiastical History in the early fourth century, sorted the books into categories (3.25): the acknowledged books (the homologoumena); the disputed but widely known books, James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John; spurious books such as the Shepherd of Hermas, the Apocalypse of Peter, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the Didache; and heretical books to be rejected outright, such as the Gospels of Peter and Thomas. Eusebius himself was undecided about Revelation, which he placed in two categories depending on the reader's view.

The first list to name exactly our twenty-seven books is Athanasius's thirty-ninth Festal Letter, written in 367 to announce the date of Easter to the churches of Egypt. He lists the books and says that in these alone the teaching of godliness is proclaimed, adding that the Didache and the Shepherd may be read by new converts but are not in the canon. In the West, the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), in which Augustine took part, gave the same twenty-seven, and Pope Innocent I confirmed a similar list in 405. These councils did not invent the list; they recorded what their churches read and forbade reading other books as Scripture in worship.

The East settled more slowly. The Syriac-speaking churches for a long time used a New Testament of twenty-two books; the Peshitta, the standard Syriac version from the early fifth century, lacks 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and Revelation, and the Church of the East still reads that shorter New Testament. Revelation was long doubted in parts of the Greek East and is still not read in the Orthodox liturgy. The Ethiopian church, in its broader canon, adds books of church order to the twenty-seven.

The Reformation reopened questions briefly. Luther, in the prefaces to his New Testament of 1522, judged Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation to be of lesser standing, famously describing James as an epistle of straw compared with the letters that most clearly preach Christ. He did not remove them, and later Lutheranism received all twenty-seven. Calvin doubted that Peter wrote 2 Peter but accepted it. The Council of Trent in 1546 confirmed the twenty-seven for Catholics, and every major Protestant confession did the same.

sections.h: Books that were read but not received
sections.body:
Some writings were valued and even read in church for a time without being received into the canon. The Shepherd of Hermas, a series of visions and parables on repentance written in Rome in the second century, was popular enough to be copied in Codex Sinaiticus after Revelation, along with the Epistle of Barnabas. Codex Alexandrinus includes the two letters attributed to Clement of Rome, the first of which is a genuine letter of the church of Rome to Corinth from about AD 96. The Didache, a short church manual of the late first or early second century, was known to Eusebius and Athanasius. These books were honored as early and orthodox but judged not to come from the apostles or their circle, and so they stayed outside the list; many churches still read them as precious early witnesses.

A different category is the gospels and acts written in the names of apostles by later groups. The best known today are the Gospel of Thomas, a collection of 114 sayings of Jesus found in Coptic among the Nag Hammadi codices discovered in Egypt in 1945, and the Gospel of Judas, published in 2006 from a Coptic manuscript of the third or fourth century. Most scholars date Thomas to the second century, though a minority argue for an earlier core; the Gospel of Judas is mid-second century at the earliest, since Irenaeus mentions it around 180. The church rejected such books because they could not be traced to the apostles, contradicted the teaching the churches had received, and were unknown or rejected in most churches. Popular claims that such books were ‘banned’ at the Council of Nicaea in 325 are mistaken: Nicaea did not discuss the canon.

Scholars disagree sharply about what the variety of early Christian writings means. Walter Bauer (Orthodoxy and Heresy in Earliest Christianity, German 1934) argued that in many regions what was later called heresy came first, and that orthodoxy was the view of the Roman church that eventually won. Bart Ehrman (Lost Christianities, 2003) popularized a version of this view, presenting the canon as the choice of the winning party. Andreas Köstenberger and Michael Kruger (The Heresy of Orthodoxy, 2010) and others reply that the books that became the New Testament are the earliest Christian writings we have, that the central convictions of later orthodoxy are already present in them, and that the alternative gospels are later and dependent. Both sides agree on the basic facts: that there were many early Christian writings, and that the church's list excluded most of them.

sections.h: What the early church looked for
sections.body:
No early council published a set of criteria, but the reasons the church gave for accepting or rejecting books can be gathered from writers such as Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Eusebius, and Athanasius. Four tests appear again and again, and they worked together rather than as a checklist.

The first was apostolicity: did the book come from an apostle or from someone closely connected to the apostles? Mark was received as the preaching of Peter and Luke as the companion of Paul, according to second-century tradition preserved by Papias and Irenaeus. This test explains why Hebrews was accepted in the East, where it was thought Pauline, before the West, and why books written in apostles' names long after their deaths were rejected when the date was recognized; Paul himself warns against a forged letter “seeming to be from us” (2 Thessalonians 2:2). The second was orthodoxy, conformity to the rule of faith, the core of apostolic teaching received in all the churches: one God the maker of heaven and earth, Jesus Christ his Son who truly became flesh, died, and rose, and the Holy Spirit. A book that denied the goodness of creation or the real humanity of Christ failed this test however apostolic its name. The third was catholicity, or wide use: was the book read in churches across the Christian world, or only in one region or sect? The fourth was antiquity: did it belong to the apostolic age, or was it recent, as the Muratorian Fragment said of the Shepherd of Hermas?

Behind these tests lay the conviction that the church was recognizing books that had already proved themselves in worship, preaching, and the lives of believers. The Gospel of John states the purpose of its own writing in terms that explain why such books were treasured: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31). Christians of different traditions account for this differently. Protestants often point to the inner testimony of the Holy Spirit by which believers recognize God's voice, a theme in Calvin and the Westminster Confession (1.4-5), Catholics to the Spirit's guidance of the church's teaching office, and Orthodox to the continuous tradition of the worshiping church. The historical process can be told in the same way by all three; what differs is the account of why it can be trusted.

Every major Christian tradition treats its canon as closed, though they close it at slightly different places in the Old Testament. The reasoning differs. Catholics and Orthodox appeal to the church's definition and tradition. Protestants appeal to the unique character of the apostolic generation: the New Testament bears witness to the once-for-all events of Christ's life, death, and resurrection, and the apostles' testimony cannot be repeated or added to by later generations, however gifted.

What if a lost letter of Paul were found? The New Testament itself mentions letters we do not have: an earlier letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:9) and the letter from Laodicea (Colossians 4:16). Most Protestant theologians answer that a genuinely rediscovered apostolic letter would raise a real question, but that God's providence in preserving the writings the church received is itself part of the doctrine of Scripture, and that nothing essential is missing. Others point out that the churches received the writings they used, not every scrap an apostle ever wrote, and that the canon is the church's rule of faith, not a complete archive.

For a new reader the practical point is simple. The canon is not a secret list drawn up by a council to suppress rivals, nor a book that fell from heaven with its table of contents attached. It is the collection that Israel and the church received, used, tested, and handed on over centuries, with a firm center from very early and debates at the edges that were real and are honestly recorded. The early Christians who argued over 2 Peter and Revelation were not indifferent to the question of what God had said; they cared about it enough to argue for two hundred years.
